title: Information flow between prediction markets, polls and media: Evidence from the 2008 presidential primaries
summary_en: Are election-eve polling errors themselves predictable? Khan and Lieli look at the 2008 Obama–Clinton Democratic primary and show that, yes, prediction-market prices contain information that helps forecast the *errors* of polls. Both cross-sectional and time-series tests indicate prediction-market prices process information faster than polls, and that media-coverage volume is a useful additional input. The result challenges the common assumption that polls are an unbiased baseline.
data_used: 2008 US Democratic Party primary state-by-state daily data on (i) prediction-market prices on Intrade, (ii) opinion-poll vote shares aggregated from major pollsters, and (iii) media-coverage volume from text counts. Identification uses Granger-causality and cross-sectional regression of poll-error on lagged market prices.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian election-forecasting, communication research, and any government / NMHH analysis that uses polling as input: the paper supports treating poll-based forecasts as systematically lagged information and combining them with market-style or media-volume data when calibrating expectations. Caveat: setting is a US primary, where prediction markets are mature; Hungarian prediction-market data is much thinner.
